title: Human Expert Evaluation of Agentic AI for EO, form F04
description:
Thank you for helping us evaluate the performance of different LLMs in Agentic AI frameworks for EO!

WHAT THIS IS
We built a benchmark to test the performance of different LLMs in agentic settings. This evaluation form is to compare the answers given by these LLMs when answering a question using different tools related to the agentic framework that we built - including different EO endpoints (Copernicus/Sentinel, Landsat), ERA5 climate data, EO Dashboard narratives, ESA science strategy documents, GIS analysis and scientific literature search.

You will be given 8 questions, and for each question you see every anonymous answer that assistant actually produced for it -- usually several, occasionally just one if only one assistant answered that particular question.

WHAT YOU DO
(About 33 minutes for this form -- your progress is saved in this browser, so it's fine to do this over more than one sitting.) The form will guide you through it, but for every question you will
1. Rate how relevant and realistic the question is for EO users.
2. Score the accuracy of each answer shown.
3. If there's more than one answer, rank them all from best to worst (skip this step when only one answer is shown -- there's nothing to compare it to).

HOW TO JUDGE ACCURACY
Judge scientific and domain correctness, and whether the answer addresses every part of the question. A minority of answers (marked "▣ image" next to the answer letter) include the actual image the assistant looked at -- check the description against it directly. For every other answer you cannot open the files or images it says it produced: treat claims that you find implausible or unsupported as errors. Do not reward length or formatting. If you cannot judge a question, say so in the comment field and give your best estimate.

Answers were produced automatically and may contain errors. Local file paths were removed from the answers. Long answers are collapsed by default — click an answer to expand it.

PRIVACY
Your name is recorded so we can follow up if needed, and is not shown to other experts. Responses are used only for the research evaluation of this benchmark and are reported in aggregate. Participation is voluntary; you can stop at any time by closing the page.

profile_fields.title: Name
profile_fields.help: So we know who a response came from. Not shown to other experts.

profile_fields.title: How would you rate your Earth Observation expertise?
Which areas are you experienced in?
choices: Climate and atmospheric data (ERA5, trace gases)
EO science strategy and scientific literature

profile_fields.title: Consent
choices: I agree that my responses are used for the research evaluation of this benchmark.

relevance.title: How relevant and realistic is this question for EO users (researchers, analysts, practitioners)?
relevance.help: 1 = not relevant or unrealistic; 3 = plausible but marginal or somewhat artificial; 5 = highly relevant and realistic.

accuracy.title: Accuracy: how correct and complete is each answer?
accuracy.help: 1 = incorrect or unusable; 2 = mostly incorrect or major omissions; 3 = partially correct or incomplete; 4 = mostly correct, minor issues; 5 = correct and complete. Equal scores are allowed.

ranking.title: Ranking: order all answers from best to worst.
ranking.help: Drag, or use the arrows, to put the best answer at the top and the worst at the bottom. Ties are not allowed.

familiarity.title: How familiar are you with the topic of this question?

comment.title: Comment (optional)
comment.help: For example: an error you spotted, why a question is not relevant, or that you could not judge it.

Manual Conversion to Celsius:
To convert the temperature from Kelvin to Celsius, subtract 273.15 from the t2m values in the NetCDF file. You can use tools like Panoply, CDO, or Python (xarray) for this conversion.

import xarray as xr

Load the NetCDF file

Subtract 273.15 to convert from Kelvin to Celsius

Save the result
ds.to_netcdf("data/era5_2m_temp_hourly_jul2023_southern_europe_celsius.nc")

items.question: Search the EO Dashboard for narratives about wildfires or burned areas. Identify the study area they discuss, then download two Sentinel-2 false-colour near-infrared composites of the affected area: one before and one after the wildfire event. Compare the images and describe visible changes in vegetation cover, burned areas, and landscape conditions associated with the fire.

answers.text:
Based on the two Sentinel-2 false-color near-infrared (NIR) composites of Southeast Australia — one taken before the 2019-2020 bushfires (November 2019) and the other after (January 2020) — the following visible changes can be observed:

1. Vegetation Cover
• Before the Fire (November 2019): The imagery shows a predominantly green and brown landscape, indicating healthy vegetation cover, particularly in the eucalyptus forests. The green tones represent areas with dense, living vegetation, while the brown areas suggest drier or less vegetated regions.
• After the Fire (January 2020): There is a significant reduction in green tones, replaced by large areas of red and dark brown. This indicates a substantial loss of vegetation cover due to the fire. The red areas represent burned vegetation, while the dark brown areas suggest charred or ash-covered land.

2. Burned Areas
• Before the Fire: No visible signs of burned areas; the landscape appears relatively intact with natural vegetation patterns.
• After the Fire: Large, contiguous areas of red and dark brown are clearly visible, indicating the extent of the burned regions. These areas are concentrated in the forested regions, particularly in New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland, which were the most affected by the fires.

3. Landscape Conditions
• Before the Fire: The landscape appears relatively uniform in terms of vegetation density, with some variation due to natural topography and land use.
• After the Fire: The landscape is visibly scarred, with large patches of burned land. The contrast between the remaining green vegetation and the burned areas is stark, highlighting the severity of the fire's impact. The burned areas appear as dark, charred patches, while the surrounding areas still retain some vegetation.

Summary
The comparison between the two images clearly demonstrates the devastating impact of the 2019-2020 Australian bushfires. The loss of vegetation cover, the extent of the burned areas, and the overall landscape degradation are evident in the post-fire image. The red and dark brown tones in the January 2020 image indicate significant ecological damage, with large areas of forest and vegetation destroyed. This visual evidence underscores the scale of the environmental impact of the fires, which affected approximately 74,000 square kilometers of eucalyptus forests across southeast Australia.

Key Observations:

• The burned areas are concentrated in specific regions, suggesting that the fires were not uniform across the entire study area.

These changes highlight the devastating impact of the 2019-2020 bushfires on the vegetation cover and landscape conditions in southeast Australia. The comparison clearly demonstrates the extent of the damage caused by the fires, with large areas of forest being destroyed and the landscape transformed into a charred, barren terrain.

The loss of vegetation cover, the extent of the burned areas, and the overall degradation of the landscape are evident. The images provide a powerful visual representation of the environmental damage caused by the fires and highlight the need for restoration efforts in the affected regions.

answers.text: I’ve routed your request to the VLM sub-agent for visual analysis of the MOOC lecture content on cryosphere remote sensing.

ESA Science Strategy Objectives on Sea Ice as a Climate Indicator
The ESA Earth Observation Science Strategy includes guiding science questions directly related to sea ice and its role as a climate indicator, such as:
• SQ-20: What are the drivers of ice-sheet and glacier mass balance and snow cover change, and what are the impacts of such changes in the Earth system?
• SQ-21: What are the physical processes that drive the sea ice state and its variability?
• SQ-24: What is the relationship between changes in Polar and high mountain regions and global climate variability?

These objectives emphasize the importance of cryosphere remote sensing for monitoring sea ice dynamics and their broader climate implications.

MOOC Lecture on Cryosphere Remote Sensing

• Radar waves penetrate freshwater ice and superimposed snow, providing detailed information on ice properties.
• Active radar sensors are invaluable for imaging large areas at high resolution, especially under poor weather or low-light conditions.
